brief.head: Bills as big data
brief.text: Offered a hero who steals his neighbours’ bills, Ajay Shah saw only one earthly rea­son to do it: “to cre­ate a data set about elec­tric­ity con­sump­tion.” {079-J01}

brief.head: Dear sister-in-law
brief.text: Bota Singh’s taunt­ing verse let­ter to Zakaria Khan ad­dressed the gov­er­nor as “my sis­ter-in-law”. Amit Varma ad­mit­ted he did not quite un­der­stand why that was an in­sult. {079-J12}

brief.head: A governor with no OTT
brief.text: Why would a gov­er­nor used to fifty thou­sand horses ride out against two men? No wars, said Amit Varma, and “no OTTs to watch. So Zakaria Khan is bored.” {079-J11}

brief.head: No more Indians

brief.head: I am the parcel

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.who: Ajay Shah, setting up his true story of children sent through the post

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah pitch four more films
lead.head: Bills, a bridge, a board and a boy

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 79

body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah have pitched sto­ries that should be films in sev­eral episodes. None of them has been made into a film yet. So Varma opened this one with an offer: “If you, gen­tle reader, are in­ter­ested in pro­duc­ing a film like that, get in touch with us, we’ll get the job done.” {079-R08}
This time there were four pitches: a man who steals his neighbours’ elec­tric­ity bills, two young Sikhs who seize a bridge, two chess play­ers across a board, and a child sent through the post.
Three were Varma’s, built from the in­side out: back­story, mo­tive, glances and props. The fourth was Shah’s, whose idea of a film, he said, is “ex­actly op­po­site”.
## A thief with a heart
The first began with a dream. The show’s cin­e­matog­ra­pher, Vaishnav Vyas, dreamt that Shah was steal­ing everyone’s pa­per­work. Varma kept the premise and built a quiet love story on it.

His hero is a geeky bach­e­lor in his early fifties who looks like Shah. He picks up his neighbours’ bills from their doorsteps. A friend in the elec­tric­ity de­part­ment cuts off those who for­get to pay, and “Ajay Bhai” gets the power back for the bill amount, a late fee and a bribe.
Then a woman moves in, too ill to leave her bed, and the grifter soft­ens. “He is human,” Varma said. “He is touched by this.” {079-S01}
Shah sug­gested ground­ing the hero in the Marxist idea of alien­ation. Varma pre­ferred to let the why show through in how the char­ac­ters live.
## A toll of their own

The sec­ond pitch was his­tory, from Sarbpreet Singh’s *Cauldron, Sword and Victory*. In 1739, with the Sikhs in hid­ing from Zakaria Khan, the Mughal gov­er­nor of Punjab, two young Sikhs, Bota Singh and Garja Singh, took an empty bridge on the road from Delhi to Lahore.
They taxed every trav­eller, taunted the gov­er­nor into rid­ing out, and died fight­ing, with one work­ing leg be­tween them.

Varma kept the events and in­vented only the inner lives: a black sheep, a re­jected suitor, two young men who did not know what they wanted. He turned their deaths into a ques­tion for ev­ery­one: what fu­tile bat­tles are we fight­ing? {079-S02}
The third pitch put the real Sultan Khan, an Indian who won the British Chess Championship in 1928, across the board from Mr B, the pris­oner in Stefan Zweig’s novella *The Royal Game*.
In Varma’s end­ing, Khan be­comes world cham­pion, then lets Mr B win, see­ing that the game he had played all his life was never the one on the board. {079-S03}
## Return to sender

Shah’s story was true. In 19th-century America, he said, the post of­fice would carry a par­cel any­where in the coun­try at mod­est prices, and one day some­one asked to post a child. The clerks weighed the child, charged the par­cel rate and pasted the ad­dress on the child’s shirt. {079-S05}
Posting chil­dren soon be­came nor­mal. For Shah, it showed how far par­ents, postal work­ers and chil­dren trusted strangers. “It speaks very well for the trust cap­i­tal of that coun­try,” he said.
Varma, asked to bring the premise to life, sup­plied a drunk fa­ther, a storm and a lonely old man in a sort­ing of­fice.
That, Shah said, is how they di­vide the work: he sets up “the rules of a sit­u­a­tion”, and it takes “a ge­nius like you” to an­i­mate it.

second.label: Bragging rights
second.head: Beat a grandmaster, once
second.deck: Amit Varma’s favourite boast, and the fine print he usually leaves out

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his one blitz win over Abhijit Kunte

body: Amit Varma often boasts that he has beaten a grand­mas­ter. It is, he ad­mit­ted, “a very dis­hon­est boast”: he was 17, and the boy across the board was 14 and not yet a grand­mas­ter. {#kunte}

The boy was Abhijit Kunte, at a chess club in Pune. He went on to be­come a grand­mas­ter, Indian cham­pion and British cham­pion. Varma beat him in one blitz game with a queen sac­ri­fice, and Kunte said: “My God, I didn’t know you could play like this.” {#queensac}
They must have played dozens of blitz games, Varma said, and he surely lost all the rest. “It is sweet joy to win even once.” {079-S04}

quote.text: I will often boast that I have beaten one grand­mas­ter in my life.

third.head: Lions, at any price

pic.caption: Amit Varma on battles fought for respect

body: A thread ran through Amit Varma’s pitches: peo­ple who fight, some­times to the death, to prove some­thing to oth­ers and to them­selves.
Bota Singh and Garja Singh seized a bridge, and died on it, be­cause a farmer had called them jack­als rather than lions. A real lion, the farmer said, would never run away or hide.

Varma’s Sultan Khan has to win every game, al­most on de­mand, be­cause ev­ery­where re­spect is at stake: “His re­spect, his father’s re­spect, his family’s re­spect, his nation’s re­spect.” {#respect}

“So many lives are lost be­cause you’re anx­ious to prove things to oth­ers, be­cause you’re anx­ious to prove things to your­self,” Varma said. {079-C06} Then he went fur­ther: “Is ev­ery­thing is ev­ery­thing a fu­tile bat­tle?”

from1.head: Bills, a bridge, a board and a boy

quote.text: I think a mis­take that main­stream films often make is they try to lo­cate the why.

box.title: Chekhov’s gun
box.text: Amit Varma ex­plained the prin­ci­ple of the Russian short-story writer Anton Chekhov: if you show a gun in the first act, it must go off by the third. In the bill collector’s story, the wires, the Maggi and her neat­ness each pay off. {079-C01}

sections.label: First reel
sections.head: Show, don’t spell it out
sections.caption: showing, not telling
body: Amit Varma set up his first film with props, not speeches. The hero’s life is set out in a glance: wires and elec­tron­ics ev­ery­where, stor­age boxes full of paper, one toaster, half a packet of bread and piles and piles of Maggi pack­ets. {#maggi}
“I’m doing a show don’t tell kind of thing here,” Varma said. Even the hero’s tea is dip-dip tea.

When the hero prom­ises his ail­ing neigh­bour dal chawal, he re­mem­bers that he can­not cook, botches it and gets some from else­where. She re­alises as she eats that he can­not have made it. {#dalrealise} They look at each other and smile. Nothing is spelt out.
## Where the why goes
Ajay Shah wanted the hero’s mo­tive grounded in the Marxist idea of alien­ation. Varma dis­agreed: the why should come through in how char­ac­ters live and act, not be stated out­right. {079-C02}

Her neat­ness, shown in her painstak­ing cook­ing, pays off in his bath­room, where she can­not leave a cup­board half-open. It “springs back out like an adamant econ­o­mist,” Varma said, and then fur­ther, “like a re­cal­ci­trant com­mu­nist”. {079-J03}

~ The hero’s hoard­ing, the film re­veals, began as a com­pul­sion: he sees paper on a doorstep and can’t help him­self. Then, as Varma put it, “somebody’s elec­tric­ity is cut and he of­fers to help and out of this emerges the busi­ness model.”

quote.text: I think a mis­take that main­stream films often make is they try to lo­cate the why.

sections.label: Second reel
sections.head: Hafta on the high road
sections.caption: rent-seeking on the bridge
body: Amit Varma’s first two pitches are both small stud­ies of rent-seeking. His bill col­lec­tor cre­ates a prob­lem and then charges to solve it. “The bug­ger is ev­ery­thing we hate about the Indian state,” Varma said. {079-C03}
On the bridge, Bota Singh and Garja Singh charged one paisa for a don­key and six for a cart. {#paisa} Every trav­eller paid.

Garja was happy with the money. Bota said they had come to be war­riors, not traders, and since no­body paid them vol­un­tar­ily, they were “like crooks or gov­ern­ment”, which to him were syn­onyms. {#crooks}
Rent-seeking usu­ally needs the state’s con­nivance, Varma said. Here ap­a­thy was enough: no­body asked who the two were, and the toll be­came nor­mal.
## The losers’ ver­sion
History is nor­mally told from the winner’s side, Varma said. The only ac­counts of the bridge come from the loser’s side, in Sikh books that treat the two men’s deaths as mar­tyr­dom. {079-C04}
~ That is why the fight reads, in his words, “like a Rajinikanth film”. Narrative bat­tles are old too: after an ear­lier clash, the Mughals and the Sikhs each claimed to have won.

quote.text: What is cu­ri­ous is that his­tory is nor­mally told from the winner’s side.

sections.label: Third reel
sections.head: The engine and the eye
sections.caption: calculation and pattern recognition
body: Amit Varma’s chess film joins a novella to a life. In Stefan Zweig’s *The Royal Game*, Mr B is held by the Nazis in soli­tary con­fine­ment with noth­ing but a chess book, and plays against an alter ego until he is in­cred­i­bly good.

Sultan Khan, the real-life Indian player, never read chess books or even talked chess with other play­ers. Varma likened him to Viswanathan Anand, who, he once wrote, was tak­ing a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race. {#maruti}
## Calculation and pat­tern

The two men stand for two routes to mas­tery. Varma cited Adriaan de Groot’s study: grand­mas­ters and novices think the same num­ber of moves ahead, but grand­mas­ters are bet­ter at pat­tern recog­ni­tion. {079-C05}

Mr B, after thou­sands of hours alone in a cell, cal­cu­lates con­crete lines al­most like an en­gine. Khan has po­si­tional sense: he can look at a po­si­tion on move eight and pic­ture the pawn struc­ture of the end­ing. {#move8}
In Varma’s end­ing, the two meet in Zweig’s match with the roles re­versed, and Khan lets Mr B win.
~ Ajay Shah re­called real matches with a psy­cho­log­i­cal edge, Fischer–Spassky and Gukesh–Ding. “Some matches are more nor­mal than oth­ers, but these matches stick out.” {079-J16}

quote.text: He de­cides that he doesn’t want to win. That he wants to let this guy take it

sections.label: Fourth reel
sections.head: In strangers we trust
sections.caption: the trust capital of a country
body: Ajay Shah pitches the other way round. He sets up the rules of a sit­u­a­tion, he said, “and then we re­quire a ge­nius like you to an­i­mate it with peo­ple and de­sires.” {079-C08}

His sit­u­a­tion came from 19th-century America, where the post of­fice cre­ated a pub­lic good: de­liv­ery of a packet any­where in the United States at mod­est prices. {#postoffice} People posted pota­toes and sacks of wheat, and the postal sys­tem moved the pack­ets around.
## No rule against it
Almost as a joke, some­one asked to post a child, and the clerks played along. As Amit Varma put it, there would have been no rule say­ing a par­cel is not al­lowed to be human. {#rule}
The child was routed from one clear­ing cen­tre to the next and, Shah thought, de­liv­ered to the grand­par­ents. Posting chil­dren be­came a nor­mal thing. {#normal}
For Shah, this said some­thing about the coun­try: par­ents, postal work­ers and chil­dren were all com­fort­able trust­ing the good be­hav­iour of strangers. {079-C07}
~ He found it “so beau­ti­ful and so mind blow­ing” that there was this level of trust cap­i­tal and good hu­mour, and that postal em­ploy­ees would feed the chil­dren along the way.

quote.text: It speaks very well for the trust cap­i­tal of that coun­try.
Are we stand­ing on one leg against the power of the state, I ask you, against the power of bad ideas? We shall con­tinue to stand, it is all we can do.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s first pitch, from a cinematographer’s dream
stories.head: Love in the time of late fees
body: It began with a dream. The show’s cin­e­matog­ra­pher, Vaishnav Vyas, told Amit Varma he had dreamt that Ajay Shah lived in a build­ing and stole everybody’s bills.

Varma kept the premise. His hero, a geeky bach­e­lor in his early fifties who looks like Shah, climbs the stairs of an old­ish build­ing that could be in Bandra East, pick­ing up the bills on every doorstep. {#bandra}

Some res­i­dents with no bill for­get to pay, and his friend from the elec­tric­ity de­part­ment cuts them off. Then the help­ful “Ajay Bhai” gets the power back, for the bill amount, a late fee and a bribe, and the two split the pro­ceeds.

A woman in her for­ties moves in alone. Her power is cut too, but she never comes to him: she is too ill to get out of bed. Touched, he gets it back and of­fers to make her dal chawal. Then he re­mem­bers, Varma said, “that like all men he has over­promised”. {079-J04}

She cooks for him in re­turn, ev­ery­thing chopped into per­fect pieces. At his flat, she tries to shut a bath­room cup­board that keeps spring­ing open, and finds his hoard of bills, her own among them.

She storms out threat­en­ing to call the po­lice, but never re­ports him. In the end she sees he meant no real harm, and he apol­o­gises clum­sily. The de­tails of how it re­solves, Varma kept back, “partly be­cause I haven’t thought of them yet”. {079-J06}
~ The last scene: door­bells ring across the build­ing, the screen splits into many doors open­ing, and every bill is there. {#lastscene} The res­i­dents dance over the clos­ing cred­its.
stories.why: Varma makes a petty rent-seeker sym­pa­thetic with­out a line of ex­pla­na­tion. Every prop, from the wires to the Maggi to her tidi­ness, is planted early so that it can pay off later, as Chekhov ad­vised. {079-C01}
stories.postscript: Vyas, who will play the rude nephew, of­fered to play the hero. Varma said no: “you’re too young and hand­some.” {079-J02}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the collector of bills

stories.kicker: From Sarbpreet Singh’s history, two Sikhs and a toll
stories.head: Two men, one leg, no retreat
body: Amit Varma’s sec­ond story turns on 27 July 1739. The Sikhs of Punjab were in hid­ing from its Mughal gov­er­nor, Zakaria Khan. Two young Sikhs, Bota Singh and Garja Singh, heard a farmer sneer that they were not lions but jack­als. {#jackals}

Stung, they took an empty wooden bridge on the road from Delhi to Lahore and levied a Khalsa regime tax. {#khalsatax} Everyone paid. Bota wanted a fight, so he sent the gov­er­nor a taunt­ing let­ter in verse.

Zakaria Khan, bored, rode out with a hun­dred horses. In the Sikh ac­counts, the two beat back wave after wave until the Mughals shot them in the legs. With one work­ing leg be­tween them, they locked arms and fought on until they died. {#onelegged}
~ Varma in­vented only their inner lives: Bota the black sheep, Garja the re­jected suitor.
stories.why: A story of alien­ation in the vein of Beckett and Stoppard: two young men who don’t know what they want die try­ing to prove some­thing, to oth­ers and to them­selves. {079-R02}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Bota Singh and Garja Singh

stories.kicker: Amit Varma joins a Zweig novella to Sultan Khan’s life
stories.head: The champion who chose to lose
body: In Stefan Zweig’s novella *The Royal Game*, Mr B sur­vives Nazi soli­tary con­fine­ment with only a chess book, play­ing an alter ego again and again.

Sultan Khan was real. Born in 1903, he mas­tered Indian chess, then the European game, and won the British Chess Championship in 1928, three times in all. {#threetimes} Then he came home and never played again.

In Amit Varma’s fic­tion, Khan’s fa­ther is the family’s black sheep, and the boy’s wins re­store his stand­ing. Every game be­comes a fight for re­spect. Khan be­comes world cham­pion, meets Mr B in Zweig’s match with the roles re­versed, and lets him win. The game he has played all his life, Varma said, “is not the game on the board. It is an­other game”. {079-S03}
~ Varma sug­gested the novella may de­serve an episode of its own. {079-R05}
stories.why: Chess here is a way of find­ing out who you are. The real con­test is the one in­side each player’s head, and see­ing that clearly can mean let­ting go of the win.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Sultan Khan and Mr B

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s true story, with Amit Varma’s improvised drama
stories.head: Handle with care: contains child
body: In 19th-century America, Ajay Shah said, the post of­fice of­fered de­liv­ery any­where in the coun­try at mod­est prices. People would post ten kilo­grams of pota­toes or thirty kilo­grams of wheat. {#kilos}
Then, al­most as a joke, some­one asked to post a child. The clerks played along: they weighed the child, worked out the charges and pasted the ad­dress on the child’s shirt. {079-S05}
The child was passed from one clear­ing cen­tre to the next like any par­cel and de­liv­ered, Shah thought, to the grand­par­ents. Soon post­ing chil­dren was nor­mal.

~ Amit Varma sup­plied the drama: a drunk fa­ther post­ing his surly son on a pub bet, a storm, and a lonely old man in a sort­ing of­fice who bonds with the par­cel. “There is no pro­to­col of who feeds a par­cel,” he said. {079-J18}

quote.text: So they weighed the child and worked out the cor­rect charges for the packet, and they said done.

stories.postscript: Shah left one ques­tion for an­other day: why uni­ver­sal de­liv­ery was a pub­lic good, not some­thing mar­kets sup­plied.

quiz.q: Whose dream gave Amit Varma the premise of a man who steals his neighbours’ bills?
quiz.a: Vaishnav Vyas, the show’s cin­e­matog­ra­pher, dreamt Ajay Shah was steal­ing everyone’s pa­per­work.

quiz.q: What, according to Amit Varma, does the bill collector share with the Indian state?
quiz.a: Rent-seeking, or hafta: he cre­ates a prob­lem and then charges to solve it.

quiz.q: What principle says a gun shown in the first act must go off by the third?
quiz.a: Chekhov’s gun, from Anton Chekhov: noth­ing in a story should be there with­out rea­son.

quiz.q: Why is the story of the Khalsa Bridge unusual among historical accounts?
quiz.a: The only ac­counts come from the los­ing side, Sikh texts that treat it as mar­tyr­dom.

quiz.q: What did Adriaan de Groot find about how far grandmasters and novices look ahead?
quiz.a: The same num­ber of moves; grand­mas­ters are bet­ter at pat­tern recog­ni­tion.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah say posting children revealed about nineteenth-century America?
quiz.a: Its trust cap­i­tal: par­ents, postal work­ers and chil­dren trusted the good be­hav­iour of strangers.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 79. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Stefan Zweig (Franz Xaver Setzer (1886-1939), public domain); Anton Chekhov (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Mir Sultan Khan (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0); Samuel Beckett (Roger Pic, public domain); Tom Stoppard (Philip Romano, CC BY-SA 4.0).

shelf.title: Waiting for Godot
shelf.creator: Samuel Beckett
shelf.why: The con­ver­sa­tions be­tween its two char­ac­ters, Vladimir and Estragon, cap­ture the alien­ation Amit wants for his two young Sikhs.

shelf.title: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead
shelf.creator: Tom Stoppard
shelf.why: Stoppard takes two of Hamlet’s friends, Shakespeare’s minor char­ac­ters, and builds a play ‘a lit­tle bit about alienation’ around them, which is the tem­plate for Amit’s pair.

shelf.title: Cauldron, Sword and Victory: The Rise of the Sikhs
shelf.creator: Sarbpreet Singh
shelf.why: Amit calls it a ‘magnificent’ and ‘excellent’ book.

shelf.title: Sarbpreet Singh Finds His Sikhism (Episode 407 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A chance to hear at length from the his­to­rian be­hind the Khalsa Bridge story.

shelf.title: The Royal Game (also published as Chess Story)
shelf.creator: Stefan Zweig
shelf.why: Zweig’s mov­ing novella about a pris­oner in soli­tary con­fine­ment who plays chess against him­self until he can beat a world cham­pion.

shelf.title: The Tamilian gentleman who took on the world
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s piece on Viswanathan Anand ris­ing with­out the Soviet school’s sys­tem­atic train­ing, like tak­ing a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race, which shows how ex­tra­or­di­nary his world-championship ca­reer was.

shelf.title: Thought and Choice in Chess
shelf.creator: Adriaan de Groot
shelf.why: De Groot’s find­ing that grand­mas­ters look no fur­ther ahead than novices but excel at pat­tern recog­ni­tion, which un­der­pins Amit’s ac­count of why the Soviet school dom­i­nated chess.

shelf.title: Seven Stories That Should Be Films (Episode 23)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The first of the show’s se­ries of true sto­ries the hosts would turn into films, and Amit’s favourite episode at the time.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28)

laughs.text: Ajay’s re­sponse to the premise of a man steal­ing his neighbours’ bills: ‘If I would scoop up the bills of peo­ple, the only earthly rea­son would be to cre­ate a data set about elec­tric­ity con­sump­tion.’

The cup­board door the ob­ses­sive-compulsive neigh­bour can’t get shut ‘springs back out like an adamant econ­o­mist,’ and when pushed again, ‘springs back out fur­ther like a re­cal­ci­trant com­mu­nist.’

Amit on male hap­less­ness. Having of­fered to cook, the hero ‘re­mem­bers that like all men he has over­promised.’ When caught with the bills, he says ‘I can explain’: ‘Have you ever been in a fight with a woman, Ajay Shah, where you have said some­thing like I can ex­plain, know­ing that you can’t? You have. An es­sen­tial part of the human ex­pe­ri­ence.’
Asked how he opens a wine bot­tle, Ajay says: ‘Oh, there have been many dis­as­ters be­cause there is no cork opener in my house.’
Amit’s posted boy, stranded in a sort­ing of­fice by a storm: ‘there is no pro­to­col of who feeds a par­cel be­cause you know, you don’t nor­mally need to feed parcels.’

Bota Singh’s let­ter to Zakaria Khan, in Sarbpreet Singh’s trans­la­tion: ‘Staff in hand on the road I stand, a penny an ass, six­pence a cart, this is a toll that I com­mand. My sis­ter-in-law, my dear Khan, a re­sponse does Bota Singh de­mand.’ Amit ad­mits he doesn’t quite un­der­stand why ‘sis­ter-in-law’ was the in­sult.

Ajay on chess matches with a psy­cho­log­i­cal edge: ‘In Fischer–Spassky there is a psy­cho­log­i­cal as­pect, in Gukesh–Ding. Some matches are more nor­mal than oth­ers, but these matches stick out.’
